items.stem: Which core dimension of responsible AI describes weighing how an AI system affects different groups of stakeholders?

options.rationale: Explainability is about understanding and evaluating what the system outputs, not about impact on groups.
Controllability is the ability to monitor and steer system behavior.
Fairness considers how the system affects different groups of stakeholders, so it matches the description.
Governance applies best practices across the AI supply chain, not group impact.

items.explanation: AWS describes responsible AI through core dimensions including fairness, explainability, privacy and security, safety, controllability, veracity and robustness, governance and transparency. Fairness is the dimension that looks at how a system affects different groups of people, which is why biased outcomes for a demographic group are treated as a fairness problem. Explainability, controllability and governance address other concerns such as understanding outputs, steering behavior and supply chain practices.

items.stem: Which responsible AI dimension refers to producing correct outputs even when the system receives unexpected or adversarial inputs?

options.rationale: Veracity and robustness cover correct outputs, including under unexpected or adversarial inputs.
Transparency helps stakeholders make informed choices about using the system, not output correctness.
Privacy and security concern appropriate handling and protection of data and models.
Controllability concerns monitoring and steering the system rather than output correctness.

items.explanation: Veracity and robustness is the responsible AI dimension that focuses on whether a system gives correct answers and keeps behaving well when inputs are unusual, noisy or deliberately adversarial. A robust system resists manipulation such as prompt attacks and does not collapse on edge cases. Safety, transparency, privacy and controllability are related but address harmful outputs, informed use, data protection and oversight respectively. items.stem: Which Amazon Bedrock capability provides configurable safeguards, such as content filters and denied topics, for generative AI applications?

options.rationale: Knowledge Bases connect models to company data for retrieval, not to filter harmful content.
Agents orchestrate multistep tasks and tool calls rather than apply safety filters.
Prompt Management helps create and version prompts, not enforce content safeguards.
Guardrails provides content filters, denied topics, word filters and other safeguards for inputs and outputs.

items.explanation: Amazon Bedrock Guardrails gives teams configurable safeguards that evaluate both user inputs and model responses. Its filters include content filters, denied topics, word filters, sensitive information filters, contextual grounding checks and Automated Reasoning checks. Guardrails can be attached to foundation model calls or used on their own through the ApplyGuardrail API, which makes them a central tool for building safer generative AI applications. items.stem: Which dataset characteristic helps a model perform well for all of the user groups it will serve?

options.rationale: Compression affects storage size and has no bearing on how well groups are represented.

options.text: Diverse and inclusive coverage of groups
options.rationale: A dataset that includes diverse, inclusive examples of all user groups helps the model serve each of them.
Encryption protects stored data but does not change representation of groups.
Ingestion speed is a performance trait unrelated to dataset fairness or coverage.

items.explanation: Responsible AI starts with data. A dataset should be inclusive and diverse, balanced across groups, and drawn from curated, vetted sources. If some groups are under-represented, the model sees few examples of them and tends to perform worse for them. Technical traits such as compression, encryption and ingestion speed matter for operations and security but do not make a dataset more representative. items.stem: A machine learning model scores very high on its training data but performs poorly on new data. Which term describes this?

options.rationale: Underfitting shows poor results on both training and new data, not strong training results.
High bias is associated with a model too simple to learn patterns, which hurts training performance too.
Overfitting means the model memorized training data and fails to generalize to new data.
Data labeling is the process of annotating data, not a model behavior.

items.explanation: Overfitting happens when a model learns the training data too closely, including its noise, so it generalizes poorly. It is linked to high variance. Underfitting is the opposite problem: the model is too simple (high bias) and performs poorly even on training data. Distinguishing the two is a common exam skill, and both lead to inaccurate predictions in production. items.stem: A generative AI model confidently states facts that are fabricated and not supported by any source. Which term describes this risk?

options.rationale: A hallucination is a fluent but false or unsupported output from a generative model.
Overfitting describes poor generalization of a trained model, not fabricated content.
Data drift is a change in input data over time, not invented facts.
Prompt caching is a cost and latency optimization, not a risk of false output.

items.explanation: Hallucinations are outputs that sound plausible but are inaccurate or not grounded in a trusted source. They create legal and reputational risk because users may act on false information. Mitigations include retrieval augmented generation, human review and Amazon Bedrock Guardrails contextual grounding checks, which compare a response with the source material and the user query. items.stem: A company wants to reduce the environmental footprint of a generative AI workload that performs a simple, well-defined task. Which approach follows responsible model selection?

options.text: Choose the largest available foundation model
options.rationale: A larger model uses more energy and is unnecessary for a simple task.

options.text: Evaluate and use a right-sized, smaller model
options.rationale: A smaller model that meets accuracy needs lowers energy use and cost, which supports sustainability.

options.text: Train a new model from scratch
options.rationale: Training from scratch consumes far more compute and energy than selecting an existing model.
Idle, over-provisioned capacity wastes energy and conflicts with efficient resource use.

items.explanation: The Generative AI Lens recommends asking whether generative AI is required at all, then selecting right-sized, energy-efficient models, and using auto scaling or serverless capacity so resources are not idle. Picking the biggest model or training from scratch increases energy use without a matching benefit when a smaller model can meet the requirement. Sustainability is therefore part of responsible model selection alongside accuracy and cost. items.explanation: Contextual grounding checks in Amazon Bedrock Guardrails compare a model response with the reference source and the user query. items.stem: A loan approval model is trained on data in which 90 percent of the applicants come from one region. Which dataset problem does this describe?

options.text: Data stored in an unsupported format
options.rationale: Format problems affect processing, not the representation of groups.

options.text: An unbalanced dataset that under-represents some groups
options.rationale: Under-represented regions give the model few examples, which can reduce accuracy for those applicants.
Curated sources are a strength; the issue here is skewed representation.
Encryption is a security control and does not explain skewed representation.

items.explanation: Balanced, diverse and inclusive datasets are a basic responsible AI practice. When one group dominates the data, the model learns patterns that fit that group and can perform worse, or produce unfair decisions, for others. The effect shows up as unequal accuracy across demographic groups. Teams address it by collecting more representative data, rebalancing, and checking performance for each group. items.stem: A model has high error on both its training data and its test data because it is too simple to capture the patterns. What does this describe?

options.rationale: Overfitting would show low training error and high test error.
Leakage typically makes test results look better than they should, not worse.
Drift develops over time after deployment, not from a model that is too simple.
A model too simple to learn the patterns underfits and performs poorly on all data.

items.explanation: Bias and variance describe two failure modes. High bias leads to underfitting: the model makes strong simplifying assumptions and misses patterns, so error is high on training and test data. High variance leads to overfitting: error is low on training data but high on new data. Both reduce accuracy, and either can hurt some demographic groups more than others. items.stem: A bank reports 95 percent overall accuracy for its loan model, but complaints suggest it rejects qualified applicants from one demographic group. Which action best reveals the problem?

options.text: Compare model performance for each demographic group
options.rationale: Subgroup analysis exposes unequal error rates that an overall accuracy figure hides.

options.text: Train the model for more epochs
options.rationale: More training does not reveal where the model is unfair and may worsen overfitting.

options.text: Publish the overall accuracy each month
options.rationale: An aggregate number is exactly what hides subgroup differences.

options.text: Add content filters in Bedrock Guardrails
options.rationale: Content filters screen harmful text and do not measure bias in a loan model.

items.explanation: Aggregate metrics can look excellent while a smaller group is treated poorly. Subgroup analysis computes the same metrics, such as accuracy and false rejection rate, separately for each demographic group so differences become visible. Tools such as Amazon SageMaker Clarify can compute bias metrics, and human review of decisions can add context. Training longer or tracking only overall accuracy does not address fairness. Word filters block specific words and phrases, such as competitor names or profanity. Contextual grounding checks serve a different purpose, detecting hallucinations, while Knowledge Bases and fine-tuning are not guardrail safeguards. items.stem: Which characteristics make a training dataset more suitable for building fair models?

options.text: It comes from a single convenient source
options.rationale: Relying on one source narrows coverage and can embed its biases.

options.text: It is as large as possible, regardless of who it represents
options.rationale: Volume alone does not fix under-representation of groups.

options.text: It includes diverse examples of all user groups
options.rationale: Diversity and inclusivity help the model serve every group.

options.text: It is dominated by the majority class
options.rationale: Imbalance leaves minority groups with too few examples.

options.text: It comes from curated, vetted sources
options.rationale: Curated sources improve data quality and make bias easier to find and fix.

items.explanation: Responsible dataset design favors inclusivity, diversity, balance and curated data sources. Diverse coverage ensures every user group appears in the data, and curated sources improve quality and traceability, including label quality. A single source, sheer volume or a dominant majority class tends to carry or amplify bias, leading to unequal model performance.
